Description
Fellowships and Internships Manager
The S.C. Sea Grant Consortium is seeking a Fellowships and Internships Manager to support the administration and coordination of the Consortium’s portfolio of student, fellowship, internship, and workforce development opportunities. The Manager will assist with recruitment, application review, participant support, communications, data management, and reporting activities while helping connect students and early-career professionals with opportunities in coastal science, management, policy, education, and outreach.
The Consortium is a state agency established to manage the Sea Grant College Program for South Carolina and based in Charleston, S.C. Our purpose is to optimize the environmental, social, and economic potential of the coastal and marine resources of the state and region through the support and dissemination of high-quality research, extension, and education programming.
Learn More About the Consortium
Primary Responsibilities
Fellowship and Internship Programs
Coordinate the day-to-day administration of the Consortium’s fellowship, internship, assistantship, and student professional development programs, including the Knauss Marine Policy Fellowship, the Katherine Sullivan Fellowship, National Marine Fisheries Service-Sea Grant Fellowship, S.C. Sea Grant Graduate Assistant Program, the Margaret Davidson Scholarship, and other opportunities as they become available.
Support the Consortium’s apprenticeship recruitment for programs such as the Commercial Seafood Apprenticeship Program.
Lead recruitment, application processing, review logistics, participant selection, onboarding, and orientation activities.
Serve as a primary point of contact for program participants and respond to routine questions regarding program requirements, logistics, and opportunities.
Coordinate communications with mentors, host organizations, universities, and program participants.
Maintain participant records, application files, and program databases.
Track participant accomplishments, placements, and alumni information.
Assist with planning and coordinating student networking events, trainings, workshops, and professional development activities.
Create and maintain student and alumni networks, facilitating communication with and among active and past students involved in Consortium programs. 
Represent the Consortium at career fairs, university events, conferences, and outreach activities promoting student and workforce development opportunities.
Program Administration and Reporting
Collect, organize, and maintain participant and program data to support agency, state, and federal reporting and institutional compliance requirements.
Maintain routine reports, summaries, and program documentation and support the preparation of program evaluations and impact reports.
Support program communications that increase program awareness and enhance recruitment by developing website content, newsletters, social media content, participant success stories, and other outreach materials in partnership with Consortium Communications staff.
Meet with faculty and students at Consortium member institutions to increase awareness and utilization of Consortium programs.
Assist with scheduling meetings, coordinating travel, and organizing program materials and events associated with the Consortium’s fellowship and internship programs.
Participate in regional and national Sea Grant fellowship, internship, and workforce development activities as appropriate.
Required Qualifications
Bachelor’s degree in marine science, environmental science, natural resource management, education, public administration, communications, workforce development, or a related field.
Experience working with students, volunteers, or early-career professionals.
Strong organizational and time-management skills, with the ability to manage multiple projects and deadlines simultaneously.
Experience maintaining data, records, or program information.
Strong written and verbal communication skills.
Ability to work independently and collaboratively as part of a team.
Proficiency with Microsoft Office and other common workplace software.
Valid driver’s license.
Preferred Qualifications
One or more years of relevant experience in program coordination, student services, education, workforce development, communications, or related activities.
Graduate assistantships, internships, and other relevant academic experiences may be substituted for professional experience.
Experience with grant-funded programs and federal, state, or university administrative systems.
Knowledge of coastal and marine issues, higher education, workforce development, or the Sea Grant network.
Experience planning meetings, workshops, trainings, or outreach events.
Position Type
Regular, full-time position. Agency hiring range: $45,000–$55,000, with final salary commensurate with experience and qualifications. The finalist for this position must successfully complete an E-Verify and driver’s license background check.
Work Location and Hours
This position is headquartered in Charleston, South Carolina. Normal Consortium business hours are Monday through Friday, 8:30 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. However, work beyond regular business hours, including evenings and weekends, may be necessary to complete the requirements of the position. Telecommuting options are available to employees following one year of employment and a review of performance. Travel throughout the state and region is necessary. A valid driver’s license is required.
How to Apply
Submit an application on the South Carolina Careers website (you must create an account to submit). Applications must include a 2-page resume, cover letter, and a list of three professional references. References will be contacted following an initial interview and with the applicant’s permission.
This position is available immediately. Applications close September 13. No phone calls please.

Employment decisions are made without regard to race, color, religion, national origin, gender, sexual orientation, gender identity, age, physical or mental disability, genetic factors, military/veteran status or other characteristics protected by law. South Carolina is making our veterans a priority for employment in state agencies and institutions. The S.C. Sea Grant Consortium participates in E-Verify.

Description
The Wilson lab in the Department of Entomology at the University of Kentucky is recruiting a PhD student in Entomology to start in Spring 2027. This position will be located in Lexington, Kentucky on the main campus of the University of Kentucky. We study sustainable insect pest management and natural enemy conservation in urban trees, shrubs, and turfgrass. The selected student would be expected to study 1) how flowering lawn weeds influence biological control of scale insects in urban trees, and 2) the degree to which lawn-applied insecticides translocate into scale honeydew in nearby trees and resultant effects on natural enemy communities. The selected student will be encouraged to develop their own research projects under the general themes of the lab.
  Ideal applicants will possess a master’s degree and have a background in entomology, ecology, environmental sciences, biology, or a related field. Exceptional candidates with only a B.S. degree may be considered as well. Prior experience with field-based data collection, scientific writing, and statistical analysis are required. Successful applicants will start in January 2027. Students will receive an assistantship which fully covers tuition and provides a competitive stipend and health insurance. Prospective applicants are encouraged to contact Dr. Caleb Wilson with questions: c.wilson@uky.edu
 The University of Kentucky is located in Lexington, Kentucky which contains a vibrant downtown along with many excellent options for dining, shopping, and outdoor recreation. The department of entomology is composed of 20 faculty with expertise in a wide array of disciplines. The department is consistently ranked as one of the most productive in the country and our students have moved on to successful careers in academia, industry, and government. Starting in December 2026, the department will be based in the newly constructed Agricultural Research Building which will contain state-of-the-art lab equipment for conducting research.
 Additional information can be found at the Wilson lab website: https://caleb-j-wilson.com/, and the University of Kentucky Department of Entomology graduate program: https://entomology.ca.uky.edu/academics/graduate. 
 Prospective students should email application materials to Dr. Caleb Wilson at c.wilson@uky.edu by September 18th, 2026. Interviews will be conducted as applications are received. Applications received after September 18th may still be considered for an interview. The selected candidate will be required to apply to the graduate school at the University of Kentucky by December 1st 2026. Candidates who apply to the graduate school without interviewing with Dr. Wilson will not be considered for this position.
 To apply, please email Dr. Caleb Wilson at c.wilson@uky.edu by September 18th, 2026, with “Scale insect grad student application: First name, Last name” in the subject line and attach the following documents:
1. A cover letter describing research experience, interests, and career goals
2. CV
3. Name and contact information for 3 professional references.
4. An unofficial transcript for all degrees received or in progress.

Project Description: The Padilla Applied Wildlife Science (PAWS) group at the University of Texas at El Paso (UTEP) is in search of a PhD student to work on population ecology and demographic modeling of an invasive ungulate (Ammotragus lervia) in the Chihuahuan Desert. The student will combine GPS telemetry data, camera trap data, and animal health data to estimate vital rates with the goal of developing population models for aoudad management. This project will include field work at UTEP’s rugged Indio Mountains Research Station along the US-Mexico Border. 
 About me and the lab: The PI - Benjamin Padilla - is an Assistant professor at UTEP with experience working in academia and for the state of Oregon’s Department of Fish and Wildlife. The PAWS group aims to use sound field and quantitative approaches to answer applied questions in wildlife ecology, management and conservation through collaboration, communication, and engagement with stakeholders. 
 About UTEP: UTEP is a Carnegie R1 (very high research activity) university with an active research community and a vibrant campus at the U.S.-Mexico border. El Paso offers unique field access to desert and mountain ecosystems, as well as a dynamic cultural environment that is often a pleasant surprise to first-time visitors. 
 To Apply: Please send a CV and a brief cover letter describing your background and why you want to pursue a PhD and your interests in the topic. Please do not send an application created with AI. 
 If you have questions about the university, the lab, or the project, check out the lab website (www.padilla-wildlife.weebly.com), or contact me, Benjamin Padilla (bjpadilla@utep.edu).

Description
The Bock Lab (https://samantha-bock.com/) at Oklahoma State University is recruiting two graduate students (MS or PhD) to join the group beginning Fall 2027. We combine approaches from ecology, developmental biology, and comparative genomics to understand how diverse animal life histories emerge and evolve. Graduate students will develop independent projects related to one of the following research areas:
Evolution of temperature-dependent sex determination (TSD) mechanisms in turtles 
Many reptiles rely on temperature to determine offspring sex. This represents a powerful system to examine how developmental processes integrate environmental signals to shape lasting patterns of phenotypic variation. This project will examine the ecological, evolutionary, and genomic processes that shape variation in thermal responses within and across turtle species with TSD. 
Epigenomic drivers of aging and life history variation in sharks & rays
Changes to the epigenome, the layer of chemical modifications that control gene activity and genome stability, are a hallmark of aging and reflect life history variation within and across species. This project will leverage life history variation in elasmobranchs (sharks, skates, and rays) to uncover molecular and evolutionary drivers of variation in aging while also developing non-lethal age markers for use in conservation contexts.

Desired Qualifications
We are seeking enthusiastic, question-driven students with interests in evolutionary ecology, developmental biology, and genomics. Previous experience with bioinformatics is not required, but students with a strong interest in developing these skills are especially encouraged to apply. 
 Funding and Program Information
Students will be supported on a combination of teaching and research assistantships in the Department of Biology at Oklahoma State University. Students are admitted through the Integrative Biology (MS or PhD) graduate program. Program details, stipend information, and admission requirements can be found here: https://cas.okstate.edu/biology/graduate_studies. Additional information about the OSU Graduate College application process can be found here: https://gradcollege.okstate.edu/application-process
 Interested students should email samantha.bock@okstate.edu. In your email please include a CV and brief statement of past research experience and future research interests. Review of materials will occur on a rolling basis beginning immediately and priority will be given to students who submit their materials by September 18, 2026. 
Contact
Samantha Bock
samantha.bock@okstate.edu (preferred contact method)

Description
The Swierk Organismal Ecology Lab in the Department of Biological Sciences at Binghamton University (SUNY) is seeking 1-2 PhD students to join the lab starting Fall 2027 or Spring 2028. Our lab is broadly interested in the function, evolution, and underlying mechanisms of traits associated with animal communication, reproduction, and predator avoidance. We study how selection and phenotypic plasticity shape these traits in heterogeneous environments. Much of our lab’s work is addressed using reptiles (primarily anoles) and amphibians in the Neotropics and in the Northeastern USA. 

The Swierk Lab seeks PhD students who are interested in developing questions that build upon our existing work in either of two research areas: 1) animal body coloration as a dynamic signal in conspecific and heterospecific communication, with an emphasis on visual modeling with respect to animal visual systems; and 2) specialized adaptations facilitating antipredator strategies, specifically the morphology, behavior, and respiratory physiology of rebreathing in semi-aquatic anoles. These projects will be developed using Neotropical anoles as a study system. 

Qualifications: 
BA/BS in related field 
Motivated, independent, collaborative 
Relevant research experience 
Demonstrated scientific writing and communication skills 
Willing to spend 2-3 summer months/year conducting research at Neotropical field stations 

Preferred candidates will also have: 
Strong statistical / quantitative skills 
Prior experience with tropical field research, animal behavior, and/or herpetology 
Completion of MS degree (though any candidate is welcome to apply)
Interest in applying for external grants/fellowships (e.g., NSF GRFP) 

Binghamton University (BU) is the top-ranked institution in the SUNY system and is consistently rated as one of the premier public universities in the Northeast. BU is included in the Carnegie Classification system's "very high research activity" (R1) category. PhD students are supported by tuition-waived teaching assistantships. Our 930-acre campus is located in the Southern Tier of New York, between the Catskills and Finger Lakes, about a 3-hour drive from NYC.  Project Title: Evaluating the likelihood of talus roost sites for monitoring western bat assemblages affected by white-nose syndrome
 The Bernard Research Lab is recruiting a graduate student to work on a Colorado Parks and Wildlife funded project. This is a collaborative project with Dan Neubaum (CPW), Dr. Paul Moosman (Virginia Military Institute) and Dr. Riley Bernard (University of Wyoming). The specific methods will include the following:
·      Hiking to remote talus fields to visually survey for bats 
·      Hand capturing bats, collecting guano, and swabbing for fungal DNA
·      Collecting data related to site metrics, bat species and sex, Pd presence, etc.
·      Working in a variety of conditions with a suite of collaborators from academic to state and federal agencies
 Project Goals:
Research efforts investigating the interplay between bat behavior and white-nose syndrome (WNS) in North America have been heavily restricted to the east. The progression of the disease across the great plains and into western states and lack of baseline ecological data for susceptible bat species in the west (e.g., roosting behaviors) create challenges for integrating effective conservation interventions. For instance, western states typically rely on testing bats for WNS during capture events conducted during spring (i.e., mist-netting efforts or sampling females at large maternity colonies) versus conducting surveys during winter in subterranean roosts which can target both males and females. 
 The goal of this study is to improve understanding of roost resources, aspects of fungal invasion biology, and disease progression of WNS in Colorado. Specifically, we will focus on three WNS-susceptible species known to inhabit high elevation talus in the Rocky Mountains (> 9,000ft above sea level) which include the little brown myotis (Myotis lucifugus), long-legged myotis (Myotis volans), and western long-eared myotis (Myotis evotis). Each species is currently listed as ‘Tier One’ species under the 2025 Colorado State Wildlife Action Plan and are expected to see elevated mortality from WNS, with M. lucifugus experiencing declines > 90% elsewhere in its range.
       Our specific objectives are to:
1.     Investigate how talus slopes are used during the active season by western bat populations and provide empirical insights regarding their importance as roost sites 

a.     Data collected will provide state and federal agencies with information regarding the life history of rock-roosting bats strengthening their ability to assess conservation and management needs.

2.     Investigate Pd presence in talus roosts during the active season and convey the degree to which state and federal agencies need to worry about its spread at these sites. 

a.     Data will specifically assess potential for male bats using these sites, thus act as WNS vectors by harboring the disease over summer and infecting females during autumn swarming or at winter hibernacula.

 Start date: The ideal candidate will start 19 January 2027 [start of the spring semester]. The first field season will be conducted from June – August 2027, second June – August 2028 and a planned graduation in either Fall 2028 or Spring 2029.
 To apply: Submit a single PDF labeled as Lastname_GradApplication_Talus.pdf containing 1) a cover letter [this should include a description about your academic career thus far, why you are interested in this project/working with bats, and your career goals], 2) a CV or resume, and 3) the name and contact information of 3 references. Applications or questions about the position should be sent to Dr. Riley Bernard at rbernar5@uwyo.edu.
 Review of applications will start immediately and will continue until filled.

·      Undergraduate degree in biology, zoology, wildlife and fisheries science or related field
·      Comfortable working in remote, high-elevation environments, on steep and uneven terrain, requiring some physical exertion and scrambling over boulders.
·      Experience camping and hiking in the backcountry
·      Interest or experience conducting field-based research
·      Experience working collaboratively in teams as well as independently
·      A valid driver’s license for at least one year and ability to drive long distances to field sites
·      Ability to drive 4WD vehicles safely in difficult conditions
 Desired Qualifications:
·      Experience studying bats
·      Rabies vaccinated
·      Experience or interest in habitat management and conservation of imperiled species

Diverse research groups, including those that are diverse in knowledge, experiences and identities, increases productivity and creativity. The Bernard Research Lab is strongly committed to increasing the representation of traditionally excluded groups and fostering a diverse, equitable and inclusive research lab.

Project: Drs. Brittany Mosher (Wildlife Ecology Research Lab) and Mark Henderson (Henderson Lab) at The University of Vermont’s Rubenstein School of Environment and Natural Resources are seeking a master’s-level graduate student to participate in research related to the movement of Spiny Softshells (Apalone spinifera) in Lake Champlain. The position is available beginning in either January or June 2027 and includes two years of funding (stipend, tuition waiver, and health insurance) in the form of both a graduate research assistantship and a graduate teaching assistantship. The student will be co-mentored by Dr. Brittany Mosher (UVM), Dr. Mark Henderson (USGS), and Dr. Luke Groff (Vermont Fish and Wildlife Department).
 Project description: The Spiny Softshell is threatened and a Species of Greatest Conservation Need in Vermont and is endangered in Quebec. Native populations of Spiny Softshells are not found elsewhere in the northeastern US. In Vermont, the species has been listed as threatened since 1987 due to shoreline habitat destruction, the rarity of suitable nesting beaches, and small adult population sizes. Spiny softshell reports primarily come from northern Lake Champlain near the mouth of the Lamoille River, in Missisquoi Bay, and recently, near the mouth of the Winooski River. It is unknown whether these three areas represent distinct subpopulations or whether they are connected. Our limited knowledge about population interchange and movement patterns impedes Spiny Softshell management and recovery decision-making. 
 This project will use the existing Champlain Acoustic Telemetry Observation System (CATOS) to understand Spiny Softshell movement patterns and population connectivity in Lake Champlain and its tributaries. The objectives of this research project are to: 1) Determine whether there is interchange between Vermont’s Spiny Softshell populations. 2) Identify Spiny Softshell movement corridors and barriers. 3) Assess whether the Spiny Softshell has recolonized the Winooski River. 4) Share research findings with K-12 students and with local partners.

Description
The School of Natural Resources and the Environment at West Virginia University is searching for a post-doctoral researcher to study the genomics of brook trout in West Virginia. Genomic tools will be used to determine population structure and diversity of native brook trout populations with an emphasis on biogeography and an assessment of hatchery influence. The researcher will also work closely with the state agency to interpret results in a management context and develop conservation strategies based on the generated data. The researcher will also have the opportunity to assist with other genomics projects in the laboratory, generate publications from existing datasets, and help mentor undergraduate and graduate students. Funding for one year will be provided.
 RESPONSIBILITIES: The post-doctoral research associate will be responsible for: 1) using bioinformatic approaches to analyze brook trout genomic data, 2) conducting genomic laboratory work as needed, 3) writing publications for peer-reviewed journals, 4) mentoring undergraduate and graduate students, 5) working with agency managers on the interpretation of results in a management context.
 QUALIFICATIONS: Ph.D. in fisheries, wildlife, genetics, or a related field.  Laboratory experience in genomic techniques and bioinformatic data analysis experience required.

Use existing field data to quantify forb establishment success and native bee floral preference, to improve conservation outcomes for bees.

Services by PDI provide support to our scientists who are highly experienced in their research fields but may not have the technical, information technology (IT), or data science experience to build digital tools that optimize research efficiency and maximize the impact of their ARS research.

Description
Texas A&M AgriLife Research
The Program Specialist II, under general supervision, performs specialist duties for a department, college, or division.

Responsibilities:

Educational Program Development and Delivery
Develop, coordinate, implement, and evaluate a comprehensive statewide Extension program addressing feral hog biology,
ecology, damage assessment, population management, and control.
•
Deliver educational programs throughout Texas for landowners, agricultural producers, wildlife managers, natural resource
professionals, County Extension Agents, and other relevant audiences.
•
Identify emerging feral hog management issues and develop • timely educational responses to stakeholder needs.
Provide technical support and subject-matter expertise to County Extension Agents and other AgriLife personnel addressing
feral hog-related questions and management concerns.
•
Assist County Extension Agents in identifying local feral hog management needs and developing programs tailored to local
conditions.


Applied Research and Result Demonstrations

Collaborate with Extension Specialists, faculty, County Extension Agents, landowners, agricultural producers, and natural
resource agencies to identify priority feral hog management questions.
•
Design, coordinate, and assist with applied research projects and result demonstrations evaluating feral hog management
techniques, technologies, and strategies.
•
• Assist County Extension Agents in developing, implementing, monitoring, and evaluating local feral hog result demonstrations.
• Collect, manage, analyze, and interpret data generated through applied demonstrations and Extension projects.
Translate findings from applied research and demonstrations into practical recommendations for landowners, producers,
natural resource professionals, and the public.
•
Collaborate with Texas A&M AgriLife Research and other research partners to facilitate the transfer of research findings into
Extension programming.


Extension Publications and Educational Materials

• Develop, write, edit, and update Extension publications addressing feral hog management and related wildlife damage issues.
Develop fact sheets, technical reports, management guides, decision-support tools, presentations, curricula, and other
educational resources.

• Translate peer-reviewed research into practical Extension recommendations and educational materials.
Digital and Social Media Outreach
Develop and contribute science-based content for AgriLife Extension websites, newsletters, social media platforms, videos,
podcasts, webinars, and other digital communication channels.
•
Work with Extension communications professionals and faculty to develop engaging content that communicates feral hog
management concepts to diverse audiences.
•
Develop timely educational content in response to emerging feral hog issues, management technologies, regulatory changes,
and stakeholder concerns.
•
Utilize digital technologies and innovative communication strategies to expand the reach and impact of feral hog Extension
programming.


Stakeholder and Partnership Development
Establish and maintain productive relationships with landowners, agricultural producers, County Extension Agents, wildlife
professionals, natural resource agencies, agricultural organizations, conservation organizations, municipalities, and other
stakeholders.
•
Collaborate with Texas Parks and Wildlife Department, USDA Wildlife Services, Texas A&M AgriLife Research, Texas A&M
Natural Resources Institute, universities, state and federal agencies, and other organizations involved in feral hog
management.
•
Serve as a representative of Texas A&M AgriLife Extension at relevant meetings, conferences, workshops, field days, and
professional events.
•
Identify opportunities for interdisciplinary collaboration involving wildlife management, agriculture, rangeland management,
water resources, economics, animal science, and other relevant disciplines.

Required Qualifications:
Bachelor’s degree in wildlife science, wildlife management, natural resources, range science, agricultural science, biology,
ecology, or a closely related field.
•
Two years of experience in wildlife management, natural resource management, agricultural production, wildlife damage
management, or a closely related field.
•
Preferred Qualifications:
Master's or non-thesis master's in wildlife science, wildlife management, natural resources, range science, agricultural science,
biology, ecology, or a closely related field.
•
Experience specifically related to feral hog biology, ecology, damage management, population control, trapping, or integrated
wildlife damage management.
•
Experience designing, implementing, or evaluating • applied field research or result demonstrations.
Experience developing Extension publications, peer-reviewed scientific publications, technical reports, or other educational
materials.
•
Experience delivering educational programs to landowners, agricultural producers, wildlife professionals, or other adult
audiences.
•
• Experience working with County Extension Agents or comparable outreach networks.
• Experience with quantitative data analysis and interpretation.
• Experience developing educational content for websites, social media, video, webinars, or other digital platforms.
Demonstrated record of professional presentations, publications, or Extension programming related to wildlife or natural
resource management.

Preferred Licenses, Certifications, or Registrations:
Remote Pilot Certificate

Required Knowledge, Abilities, and Skills:

The successful candidate should demonstrate:

• Demonstrated knowledge of wildlife biology and management principles.
• Demonstrated ability to communicate effectively with diverse audiences through oral and written communication.
Demonstrated ability to work independently and collaboratively with faculty, staff, agents, landowners, producers, and other
stakeholders.
•
• Ability to organize and manage multiple projects and priorities.
• Ability to use standard word processing, spreadsheet, presentation, database, and online communication technologies.
• Understanding of wildlife damage management principles and their application to agricultural and natural resource systems.
• Ability to translate scientific information into practical recommendations for nontechnical audiences.
• Strong organizational and project-management skills.
• Ability to develop and maintain collaborative relationships with diverse stakeholders.
• Ability to interpret scientific literature and communicate research findings accurately.
• Ability to work effectively both independently and as part of interdisciplinary teams.
Ability to travel extensively throughout Texas and occasionally outside the state and work occasional evenings, weekends, and
extended hours associated with educational events and field activities.

Preferred Knowledge, Abilities, and Skills:

The successful candidate should demonstrate:
Strong knowledge of feral hog • biology, ecology, behavior, and management.
• Knowledge of integrated feral hog damage management and population control strategies.
• Ability to design, implement, and evaluate applied field demonstrations.
• Ability to develop innovative educational programs and materials.

Description
TWDB Coastal Science Program is seeking to hire a full-time ecologist (TWDB 26-135) focused on modeling ecological impacts of freshwater inflows on the bays & estuaries along Texas's gulf coast. The position has a hybrid work schedule, requiring 24hrs/wk at TWDB offices in downtown Austin.


GENERAL DESCRIPTION


Performs moderately complex (journey-level) ecological data analysis and modeling work for the Surface Water Division. Work involves developing, maintaining, and applying statistical and ecological models to support freshwater inflow needs and environmental impact analysis, water resources planning, and oil spill response. Investigates, develops, and implements the use of quantitative methods and data for hydro-ecological modeling and analyses. Provides technical support in the planning, execution, and summary of scientific and engineering field studies of state streams, rivers, bays, and estuaries. Attends public meetings and provides technical support to stakeholders and customers. Communicates modeling analyses and study results to general and technical audiences. May train others. Works under general supervision, with limited latitude for the use of initiative and independent judgment. Reports to the Manager of the Coastal Science Department.


ESSENTIAL JOB FUNCTIONS

Conducts statistical data analysis and ecological modeling of state surface water resources, primarily to evaluate freshwater inflow needs and impacts for Texas estuaries.
Investigates, develops, maintains, and applies quantitative ecological methods, data, and models.
Assists with implementation of ecological modules for hydrodynamic models of Texas estuaries.
Conducts systematic and comprehensive literature reviews on related topics such as coastal ecology, modeling, and oil spills.
Initiates scientific studies including the development of detailed scopes of works for contracted studies.
Performs and leads existing or new outreach programs initiated by the Coastal Science Department.
Writes, executes, and maintains relevant R, Python, and ArcGIS programs and scripts.
Writes, reviews, and evaluates technical memos, reports, work process, and policy documents.
Develops, coordinates, and conducts program outreach activities targeting key stakeholders.
Delivers presentations on study results to technical and non-technical audiences.
Works with other departments to post updates of data and publications to the agency website.
Provides data, models, information, and technical support to stakeholder groups, scientific committees, and customers.
Serves as subject matter expert for research and monitoring contracts.
Participates in field studies, including planning, on-site work, and data acquisition, management, and analysis.
Maintains confidential and sensitive information.
Ensures individual and team files (electronic and hard versions) are appropriately maintained and timely disposed of in accordance with the agency's records retention procedures and schedule.
Maintains required certifications and licenses and meets the continuing education needs and requirements of the position to include, attending mandatory training courses.
May be required to operate a state or personal vehicle for business purposes, including the transport and operation of boats and equipment.
May perform work outdoors on boats and possibly during inclement weather or under hot and cold temperatures.
Performs other duties as assigned

MINIMUM QUALIFICATIONS

Graduation from an accredited four-year college or university with a bachelor's degree in Biology, Ecology, Hydrology, Oceanography, Environmental Science/Engineering, or a related field
Two years of relevant work experience in statistical or quantitative modeling and analysis of biological communities, population dynamics, ecosystems, or similar topics.
Experience with scientific programming in Python or R.
Relevant education and experience can be substituted for each other on a year-for-year basis.

PREFERRED QUALIFICATIONS

Graduate degree, or working towards completion of a graduate degree, in from an accredited college or university in Biology, Ecology, Statistics/Data Science, Oceanography, Environmental Science/Engineering, or a closely related field.
Three or more years of experience in statistical or quantitative modeling and analysis of biological communities, population dynamics, or ecosystems, with an emphasis on estuarine, coastal, or marine ecosystems.
Experience with advanced statistical methods, including hierarchical Bayesian modeling, multivariate statistics, and/or spatiotemporal statistics.
Experience in linking hydrological, hydrodynamics, water quality, or nutrient analyses or models into ecological modeling/analysis systems.
Experience in mechanistic ecological modeling, such as biophysical or food-web models.
Advanced programming/computational abilities including experience with probabilistic programming (PyMC, Stan, NIMBLE, or similar HMC/MCMC methods), data visualization tools (Matplotlib, Seaborn, ggplot2), and dashboard creation (PowerBI, Shiny, Streamlit)
Experience in project management and stakeholder outreach/engagement.
Strong data management and technical skills including demonstrated experience with Git/Github and Unix/Linux command line workflows.

Description
*Applications are reviewed on a rolling-basis.

ARS Office/Lab and Location: A research opportunity is currently available with the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA), Agricultural Research Service (ARS), National Animal Disease Center (NADC) in Ames, IA..

The Agricultural Research Service (ARS) is the U.S. Department of Agriculture's chief scientific in-house research agency with a mission to find solutions to agricultural problems that affect Americans every day from field to table. ARS will deliver cutting-edge, scientific tools and innovative solutions for American farmers, producers, industry, and communities to support the nourishment and well-being of all people; sustain our nation’s agroecosystems and natural resources; and ensure the economic competitiveness and excellence of our agriculture. The vision of the agency is to provide global leadership in agricultural discoveries through scientific excellence.

Research Project: The National Animal Disease Center in Ames, IA, is the American farmer's one-stop shop for animal health, food safety, and disease research. We have the experience, expertise, and biosecurity needed to work with all economically important livestock, poultry, and wildlife—from chickens to bison and everything in between. A fellowship opportunity for a post-graduate is available with the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA), Agricultural Research Service (ARS), National Animal Disease Center (NADC) in Ames, IA. The opportunity is in the Ruminant Diseases and Immunology Research Unit, which conducts basic and applied research on bovine respiratory disease and foreign Mycoplasma species that are biosecurity concerns. You will help investigate the mechanisms of pathogenesis and pathogen-host interactions of Mycoplasma mycoides subsp. mycoides (Mmm), the causative agent of contagious bovine pleuropneumonia. You will help perform laboratory activities promoting biosafety, identifying the persistence of bacterial colonization from collected samples, and assessing the presence/absence of bacteria from infected tissues. Description
Life Net Nature Ecuador Bird Monitoring Expedition A Cost-share Volunteer Training Experience

Learn or improve bird banding and monitoring skills in the tropical Andes mountains of western Ecuador. Help advance science about tropical montane forest bird communities. Learn how to collect data to determine community and species-level responses to deforestation, forest recovery, forest fragmentation, and landscape and climate changes. Your participation helps sustain an important protected area in the mega-diverse Choco Endemic Bird Area (EBA). 

Cost-share volunteers/trainees assist Dr. Dusti Becker with long-term avian monitoring and conservation in the Andes at the beautiful forest protected area, Reserva las Tangaras.  In exchange volunteers receive experience-based training in mist netting and bird banding, including the use of Hall traps and practice with some aspects of hummingbird banding. 

Team Dates:     December 7-20, 2026 (1 position available)

Where:  Reserva Las Tangaras, a 130-acre nature preserve, boasts more than 25 species of hummingbirds, dozens of colorful tanagers, the largest regional Andean cock-of-the-rock display lek, along with over 300 tropical bird species, many of which are Choco and Andean endemics. During the expedition, LNN teams typically detect around 175 - 200 different species of birds in the reserve and study area. Team members will see additional bird species while traveling to and from the project site. The reserve is also home to endangered capuchin monkeys, spectacled bears, cougars, and myriads of other wildlife species, including several rare and endangered reptiles and amphibians. 

Activities: Volunteers are trained (or refreshed on) setting up and monitoring mist nets, extracting birds from nets, carrying birds from nets to a banding station, and recording ornithological and ecological data in the field. Volunteers are also trained to band birds and make standard measurements of birds. Volunteers also learn about Hall trapping and banding hummingbirds. The site is rugged, requiring above average fitness including: ability to hike on steep, potentially muddy and slippery terrain, and cover 2-4 miles on foot each day. Back or joint impairments, or obesity may make the project too challenging for some. 

Volunteers will have time to explore the Mindo area, and the team visits higher-elevation Bellavista Cloud Forest Reserve on the last day before returning to Quito. The December team will participate in the Mindo Christmas Bird Count (CBC), which typically wins first or second place globally for bird species counted. 

Food and Lodging: Accommodation is in a spacious research cabin, where each participant has a single bed mattress with mosquito netting, pillow, and fitted sheet. Two showers with hot water and flush toilets provide comfortable field accommodations. Meals are delicious, home-style Ecuadorian, prepared by excellent cooks, and vegetarian diets can be accommodated. 

COST: Your contribution of $2450 covers transportation during the field project to and from Quito,Ecuador, meals at RLT, lodging at RLT, reserve entrance fees, salaries for Ecuadorian cooks and para-biologists, leader's costs, and a special lunch at the Bellavista Reserve. Airfare to and from Quito, Ecuador and expenses in Quito before and after the expedition are not included. Meals away from RLT during project day off are not included. 

Your cost-share helps sustain Reserva las Tangaras, supporting year-round stewardship, educational programs, outreach materials about cloud forest wildlife, maintenance of trails and signs, cabin repairs, and feeding of resident hummingbirds. Cost-share donations are used to operate the 2-week field expedition: providing the team with food, shelter, training and transportation, as well as purchasing new project equipment and supplies. 

This exciting conservation expedition begins and ends in Quito, Ecuador. 

Contact Dr. Dusti Becker, dustizuni@yahoo.com, for further details and to obtain a Life Net Nature volunteer application form. 

Qualifications: Experience with banding and mist-netting are desirable, but not required. We provide training. Students and recent graduates will benefit from this great resume building experience. Professionals and retirees in field biology, will enjoy the "field camp" experience and are much appreciated for their co-mentoring and experiences they share. All participants have the option of using the > 20 year project database for research publications, undergraduate projects, or graduate degrees.  

Visit https://lastangaras.wordpress.com/who-are-we/ for more details about Life Net Nature and Reserva Las Tangaras.  

To apply: Email Dr. Dusti Becker a brief cover e-mail detailing your experience and interest in participating on a given team. Send to dustizuni@yahoo.com. (Resume optional and helpful).  Dr. Becker will send you an official Life Net Nature volunteer application form.

ARS Office/Lab and Location: A research opportunity is currently available with the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA), Agricultural Research Service (ARS), Pacific West Area (PWA) at the Temperate Tree Fruit and Vegetable Research Unit located in Wapato, Washington.

The Agricultural Research Service (ARS) is the U.S. Department of Agriculture's chief scientific in-house research agency with a mission to find solutions to agricultural problems that affect Americans every day from field to table. ARS will deliver cutting-edge, scientific tools and innovative solutions for American farmers, producers, industry, and communities to support the nourishment and well-being of all people; sustain our nation’s agroecosystems and natural resources; and ensure the economic competitiveness and excellence of our agriculture. The vision of the agency is to provide global leadership in agricultural discoveries through scientific excellence.

The unit focuses on developing novel biological, molecular, and bio-intensive methods to control insect pests and plant pathogens affecting temperate tree fruits (apples, pears, and stone fruits like sweet cherries) and vegetable crops. 

For more information on the agency, visit the USDA Agricultural Research Service Home Page.

Research Project: You will engage in a collaborative research initiative focused on evaluating therapeutic interventions against Cherry X-disease (Candidatus Phytoplasma pruni), a major threat to sweet cherry and stone fruit production in the Pacific Northwest.

Under the mentorship of USDA-ARS research scientists, you will gain hands-on experience utilizing an in vitroplant tissue culture and molecular screening platform to evaluate candidate therapeutic compounds (such as EPA-registered antimicrobials, antimicrobial peptides, or biologically active molecules) for their efficacy in suppressing phytoplasma titers.

Micropropagation & Plant Tissue Culture: Participating in the maintenance, subculturing, and propagation of micropropagated in vitro cherry plantlet culture systems under sterile laboratory conditions.

Molecular Diagnostics & Quantification: Collecting plant tissue samples and performing molecular diagnostic assays, including DNA/RNA extractions, end-point PCR, quantitative real-time PCR (qPCR), and reverse transcription qPCR (RT-qPCR) to quantify pathogen dynamics and gene expression.

Data Analysis & Synthesis: Learning to process, analyze, and interpret diagnostic dataset outputs using statistical tools and software to compare treatment efficacy and phytoplasma titer reductions over time.

Scientific Communication & Collaboration: Collaborating with interdisciplinary research teams, presenting findings during internal research updates, and contributing data synthesis for peer-reviewed journal articles, conference presentations, and technical reports.

This opportunity is designed to enhance your professional and technical skills in molecular plant pathology, bio-assay design, and sustainable crop protection methodologies in alignment with the scientific mission of the USDA-ARS.

Description
 The Benson Lab of Predator-Prey Ecology at the University of Nebraska is seeking a highly motivated ecologist interested in playing a lead role in exciting, cutting-edge research on spatial ecology, population dynamics, and predator-prey interactions involving elk in Nebraska. There is a large amount of well-organized data available that will facilitate multiple high quality publications for someone interested in impacting the literature in the top journals in basic and applied ecology. 

From 2022-2026, we collected an intensive dataset from all core populations of elk across the state occupying areas of varying degrees of human disturbance, different predators, and considerable landscape heterogeneity. The data include detailed movement, survival, and cause-specific mortality data from ~230 GPS-collared adult male and female elk. We also have extensive trail camera data from some portions of the study area that are suitable for estimating density and investigating other questions. We work closely with researchers at NGPC who track mountain lions with GPS collars in our study area. We have developed concurrent risk surfaces derived from fine-scale data on mountain lions that can be included in the elk analyses to understand interactions with this naturally recolonized top predator at the easternmost extent of its range. The work will directly inform elk management in Nebraska and contribute to a better understanding of the basic ecology of the species and ungulates in general. If this sounds like fun – please contact me soon! 

The initial appointment will be for one year. Main duties will include data analysis, manuscript writing, and publishing results in scientific journals. In addition to elk research, the successful candidate will be expected to play a positive role in our lab group. There are opportunities to collaborate with faculty and students on other publications involving large carnivores, ungulates, and other species. This position provides excellent opportunities for publishing, networking with a variety of university and agency research groups, and professional development. 

Qualifications: PhD in Wildlife, Ecology, or related field. A strong track record of research excellence that includes publishing, strong quantitative and coding skills (especially R), and writing are expected. A passion for basic and applied wildlife ecology are required. Although previous research experience with large mammals may be beneficial it is certainly not required and ecologists with experience with other taxa are encouraged to apply. 

Above all we seek an ecologist that will be a good fit for our lab group who brings a high level of motivation to do excellent science, see work through to publication in the top journals, and ask important questions about wildlife. 

Please email the following as a single PDF attachment to John Benson at jbenson22@nebraska.edu: 1) cover letter, 2) current CV, 3) contact info for 3-5 professional references, and 4) PDFs of up to 3 peer-reviewed articles published if available. Desired start date is as soon as possible but later start dates will be considered. Please apply soon if interested!

Description
Two Master of Science (MSc) positions are available at Auburn University (start date: January 2027). Students will be hosted by the Crustacean and Molluscan Ecology lab (P.I. Dr. Jim Stoeckel; https://agriculture.auburn.edu/directory/profile.php?id=jas0018) and the Aquatic Reproductive Physiology lab (P.I. Dr. Ian Anthony Ernest Butts; https://ianaebutts.wixsite.com/labsite) in the School of Fisheries, Aquaculture and Aquatic Sciences (SFAAS). 
 Responsibilities and tasks: Procambarus clarkii (Red Swamp Crawfish) are simultaneously desired as an aquaculture product and reviled as an invasive species worldwide. Aquaculture practices to efficiently produce crayfish while minimizing risk of escapement and establishment of invasive populations are urgently needed. The successful candidate(s) will join a collaborative project involving Auburn University (USA), Ben Gurion University (Israel) and the USGS to develop techniques for efficient crayfish production in indoor recirculating aquaculture systems (RAS), investigate genetic and physiological mechanisms controlling sexual development, and produce neofemales (genetic males that develop into functional females) for production of all-male broods and invasive species control. Student(s) will develop and refine indoor production strategies for P. clarkii during critical life-history stages. They will also provide genetic and histological samples as well as life-history information to developmental physiologists and population modelers at collaborating institutions. Student(s) will use RAS production systems at Auburn University to conduct basic and applied research to better understand developmental, physiological, and behavioral functions associated with crayfish development and reproductive behavior. Studies will focus on optimizing environmental factors (i.e., habitat, photoperiod, temperature) in RAS systems. This may include use of novel aquatic x terrestrial combinations as P. clarkii typically use a combination of aquatic and terrestrial habitat during their reproductive cycle.
 Qualifications: We are looking for motivated candidates with a BSc in biology or similar discipline, knowledge of aquatic ecology and/or physiology, ability to carry out goal-oriented work, ability to work well with peers and collaborating institutions, and ability to obtain US driver’s license and vehicle. Must be legally authorized to work in the United States. Experience in reproductive physiology and/or husbandry experiences with crustacean decapods will be considered a strong asset.

Further information: please contact Dr. Jim Stoeckel (jas0018@auburn.edu) and Dr. Ian Butts (iab0007@auburn.edu).

The successful applicant will perform a variety of laboratory research tasks to support multiple current and future research projects for the Wyoming Game and Fish Department’s Veterinary Services Unit. Primary responsibilities will include optimization and application of real-time quaking-induced conversion (RT-QulC) assay for chronic wasting disease (CWD). The technician will lead a project looking to characterize prion kinetics using biological samples from a controlled longitudinal research study. The technician will also assist with other research projects, which aim to improve ante-mortem CWD detection by RT-QuIC, and investigate CWD shedding dynamics in elk. Some travel may be required for diagnostic sample collection in the field.

We are seeking a research intern (6 – 9 months) to assist with grassland and wetland ecology, biogeochemistry, and range management research. The research intern will be supervised by Dr. Grégory Sonnier & Dr. Amartya Saha. Archbold Biological Station and its partner site University of Florida Range Cattle Research Center (UF RCREC) are part of the Long-term Agroecosystem Research Network (LTAR https://ltar.ars.usda.gov ), a network of 19 agroecosystems across the United States that seek to address the grand challenge of maintaining multiple ecosystem services in food production systems. 

Archbold Internships are unpaid appointments without an entitlement to a paid job at the conclusion of the internship. $530 expense stipend, paid bi-weekly and subject to self-employment tax 
Interns receive paid time off in accordance with the Archbold Internship Policy
Gratis lodging on a working cattle ranch

Get the opportunity to work on a variety of projects, including wetland restoration and management, precipitation manipulation to simulate the effects of drought and flooding, and water retention on ranchlands. (see our two documentaries "Cowboys & Scientist" "Science of a Florida Ranch").
Experience life on a cattle ranch in a collaborative environment
Dedicate remaining time to designing and implementing an independent research project that fits within our research program, with a report and a presentation at the end of internship.

Work an average of 20 hours per week on assigned duties while being mentored.

Present a research Seminar at the end of the internship based on independent research project and submit a final copy of the report at the end of the internship.

Description

Faculty Research Assistant
(Environmental Social Science)
Oregon State University Department of Fisheries, Wildlife and Conservation Sciences
 
The Conservation and Human Wellbeing Lab, part of the Human Dimensions Lab in OSU’s Department of Fisheries, Wildlife and Conservation Sciences, seeks an interdisciplinary environmental social science Faculty Research Associate (FRA) to manage a large, NOAA-funded investigation of the social and cultural impacts of Harmful Algal Blooms.
 
Harmful algal blooms can affect coastal communities through disruptions to fisheries, aquaculture, recreation, tourism, cultural practices, public health, and access to coastal resources. This multi-institutional project will examine how these effects are experienced and distributed across communities in Puget Sound, Washington, and the Santa Barbara Channel, California. The project combines surveys, interviews, focus groups, geospatial analysis, and analysis of digital and social-media data and will produce both peer-reviewed scholarship and practical, user-oriented resources for coastal communities and decision-makers.
 
Start date: October 15, 2026
Job Location: Applicant must reside in either Corvallis, Oregon or the Puget Sound, Washington.  Location will be negotiated. 
Job Type: Full time, annual renewal depending on performance and funding
Work setting:  Office, daily use of computer required
Schedule: Monday-Friday, 8-5 (flexible 40hrs/week) 
Travel requirements: Infrequent overnight travel for meetings, and occasional lengthier trips (up to 1 or 2 weeks) to oversee field work.
Salary: $65,000
Closing: September 18, 2026 for initial review
 
Funding: Annual position with up to two additional years depending on performance.  Funding includes salary, benefits, and research expenses.  Funding is from the NOAA Socio-Economic Effects of Harmful Algal Blooms program.
 
Description: 
Bring your research and project management skills in environmental social science. You will:
Work collaboratively with three PIs based at different universities to refine and implement research plans, identify and implement steps for meeting project goals, and coordinate project activities to meet scientific and grant-related objectives.
Collect data and oversee student data collection in the Puget Sound, Washington, including Hood Canal, Bellingham Bay, and Quartermaster Harbor.  Methods will include geospatial analysis of existing datasets, public-beach encounter surveys, shoreline homeowner surveys and interviews, focus groups, and social media large data analyses.
Lead analysis of project components.  
Lead or co-lead outputs of project components, including at least one peer-reviewed manuscript as well as more creative, user-focused products
Mentor one MS student to complete independent research projects as part of overall project
Facilitate and support an external advisory group comprising managers and stakeholders to provide feedback on project implementation and outputs
Act as project manager, organizing research team, providing work reports and managing project timelines and deliverables.
Perform other related duties consistent with the position classification, project objectives, and evolving research needs as identified by the PIs in consultation with the project team.


Position Duties:

60%  Research: Conduct and oversee data collection, analysis, and reporting.

25%  Project management: Prepare reports for granting agency and collaborators, manage project budget and timeline, ensure IRB approvals, etc.

10%  Team Coordination: Coordinate and facilitate meetings with project team and advisory group

5% Mentorship:  Supervise OSU undergraduate and MS student researcher

Minimum, Required Qualifications
Graduate degree in environmental social sciences (geography, planning, psychology, anthropology, environmental studies, etc.) or related fields that included social scientific research methods, analyses, and products
Exceptional organization and project management skills 
Outstanding communication skills based in curiosity, self-awareness, and collaboration
Knowledge of ethical and methodological best practices in social scientific research
Proficiency in or capacity to quickly learn quantitative and qualitative analyses with some support (regressions, topic modeling, hierarchical clustering)
Computing skills, including statistical software & cloud-based file sharing   
Professional competence in coordinating and facilitating stakeholders and interdisciplinary science teams in a respectful and efficient manner
Demonstrated proficiency in professional writing 
A demonstrable commitment to promoting and enhancing diversity and inclusion in environmental management
Completion of a Motor Vehicle History Check

Highly Desired Qualities: 
Experience managing a large research program with multiple researchers and sub-projects
Experience mentoring student researchers
Demonstrated proficiency in writing peer-reviewed manuscripts and/or accessible white papers, reports, and other forms of visualization to communicate the role of social science in conservation/restoration to diverse audiences
Experience with encounter surveys, focus groups, scientific interviewing, geographically-weighted regressions, and/or the use of AI for large data analyses (e.g., topic modeling) 

 

To apply:

Please submit all materials to the OSU online application portal. Job requisition number JR0000719.

Please submit a CV with the names of 3 references and a cover letter describing your interest and how your experience fits the duties of the project.  Application review will begin September 14, 2026 and continue until the position is filled.

Description
Title- Waterfowl Survey & Sea Duck Specialist
Classification- Fish and Wildlife Biologist 4
Job Status- Full-Time - Permanent
WDFW Program- Wildlife Program
Duty Station- This position may be based in either Olympia, Washington, or Stanwood, Washington, depending on the successful candidate.
Please note- This position is eligible for an additional 15% pay differential when the incumbent is performing flight duties as noted in the duties listed below. 

Learn more about being a member of Team WDFW! 


The WDFW Waterfowl Section advances natural resource conservation by monitoring waterfowl populations, conducting research, and translating findings into effective management and policy.

In this position, you will shape conservation strategies, communicate research findings, and lead biologists and technical staff in efforts to sustain healthy waterfowl populations and the habitats they depend on. 


What to Expect- 
Among the varied range of responsibilities held within this role, the Waterfowl Survey & Sea Duck Specialist will, 

Design and implement study and survey protocols to determine waterfowl status and harvest: 
Plan and coordinate statewide aerial surveys to collect data on waterfowl abundance, distribution, habitat use, and productivity.
Evaluate aerial survey methods and recommend improvements to increase data quality and efficiency.
Plan and conduct vessel-based surveys to monitor marine waterfowl populations, habitat use, and distribution.
Operate or oversee operation of research vessels in support of biological surveys, ensuring safe and effective field operations.
Direct, develop, and manage data collection, research, and report writing for statewide breeding waterfowl pairs, brood production, winter status surveys, sea duck and marine waterfowl ecology, population, biology and demography, population structure and delineation, habitat associations and foraging and trophic interactions. 

Compile and analyze scientific literature and data to inform waterfowl management activities:
Maintain and update historic statewide sea duck databases for inventory and harvest. 
Compile and coordinate submission of Western Washington banding schedules for the statewide banding permit. 

Prepare professional reports and presentations to communicate findings to stakeholders, managers and decision makers about waterfowl management, status, trends, and research:
Prepare annual statewide sea duck project reports. 

Suggest or recommend decisions and options to conserve waterfowl and wetland resources to Waterfowl Section Manager:
Make policy and program recommendations as completed staff work to ensure waterfowl and wetland resources are adequately considered in multiple-resource management. 

Develop plans and procedures to implement policies for conservation and improvement of waterfowl habitat:
Provide technical expertise and analysis for evaluating migratory bird stamp/artwork proposals and in the development of expenditure plans. 
Develop proposals and write grants to support waterfowl/wetland habitat and research from external funding sources,


Working Conditions:

Work setting, including hazards:
Field work (~65%)  
Field work can vary depending on season and requires working outdoors during inclement weather, including travel to and from field sites.
Field surveys are conducted by helicopter, fixed-wing aircraft, vehicle, marine vessels (Class A, I, and II) and on foot. 
Aerial surveys are conducted at low-level, over water and land. 
Vessel surveys and captures are conducted during all seasons and will include inclement weather. 
Work on foot in the field includes walking over rough terrain while carrying light to moderate loads. 
Captures on rivers include wading in moving riverine waters. 
This position may involve working in or near water, including tasks that require navigating, negotiating, and performing duties related to water environments.
Office Work (~35%)  
Office hazards may include working under fluorescent light, repetitively entering data into computer, looking at computer monitor sitting or standing for extended periods of time. 

Schedule: Typically, Monday – Friday from 8:00 A.M. – 5:00 P.M. and may be expected to adjust the work schedule to meet business needs. A flexible work schedule will be considered at the incumbent’s request, subject to supervisory approval.

Travel Requirements: Periodic statewide or regional travel is required, dependent upon meeting time sensitive field work and project needs.
 
Tools and Equipment: Project equipment and tools, including aerial survey gear, boats (Class A, I, and II), and capture equipment. Rocket netting, at-sea captures, mist nets, and net guns for the safe capture of migratory birds
 
Customer Interactions: Frequent contact with other agency staff, cooperators and periodic interaction with the public.


Required Qualifications:

Option 1: All the following (experience may be gained concurrently):
Bachelor’s degree in wildlife management, conservation biology, wildlife ecology, natural resources science, or a related field. 
Five (5) years of professional experience in wildlife management or wildlife research, with an emphasis on waterfowl species expertise. 
Two (2) years of demonstrated knowledge of and professional experience with: 
Waterfowl survey, monitoring, and research techniques.
Waterfowl captures and handling techniques in at least one of the following - freshwater, estuary or marine environments.
Collecting, recording, and managing biological data during aerial or boat survey operations.

Option 2: Four (4) years of professional experience as a Fish & Wildlife Biologist 2 (or higher) predominately working with waterfowl species.

Please Note:
A Master’s degree in an applicable field of study may substitute for one (1) year of the required experience provided the field of major study was in wildlife science, wildlife management, or similar natural resource-related field related to species expertise. 
A PhD.  in an applicable field of study may substitute for two (2) years of the required experience provided the field of major study was in wildlife science, wildlife management, or similar natural resource-related field related to species expertise.


Certifications/Licenses:
Valid Driver’s License.


Special Requirements/Conditions of Employment:
The following are agency facilitated/provided:
Certification to participate in aerial flight surveys within 12 months of employment.
Motorboat Operator Training Course (MOTC) certification (scheduled to be obtained within 12 months of hire if the incumbent has not yet completed this training).
Ability to obtain subpermittee status on station with US Geological Surveys (USGS) Federal Bird Banding Laboratory permit within six (6) months of hire.


Preferred Qualifications:
In addition to the required qualifications, our ideal applicant will possess one or more of the following:

Prior or current subpermittee status on a Federal Bird Banding Laboratory permit.

Certification/License:
Successful completion of a Motorboat Operator Training Course (or equivalent).
Successful completion of an Aviation Egress Course (or equivalent).

Experience:
Safely operating motor vehicles.
Operating boats in marine environments (Class A, I, and II).
Navigating and independently conducting aerial bird surveys from helicopter and fixed-wing platforms, including more than 500 flight hours.
Lead and coordinate efforts of scientific expert teams in research, monitoring, and planning projects. 

Knowledge of:
Ecology and biology, species distributions, and habitat associations of freshwater and marine waterfowl species of Washington, particularly sea duck species.
Contract development and administration.
Mathematical reasoning and understanding of statistical methods and study design.
Negotiating management agreements with stakeholders and landowners.
Advance knowledge of specific species and habitat behaviors, characteristics and needs.
Researching and gathering information for scientific studies.
Advanced computer skills for modeling and forecasting.

Ability to:
Identify duck, goose, and swan species, including the classification of the species, sex, and age of individuals for monitoring and analysis purposes.
Identify and prioritize key research and monitoring need for sea ducks identified as Species of Greatest Conservation Need (SGCN) conservation and recovery.
Conduct effective oral presentations at scientific conferences, agency meetings, and public meetings.
Write, edit, and publish professional documents and reports.
Produce GIS products, including sharing databases and map products.
Coach and mentor staff to maximize success on the job.
Willingness to perform and lead aerial and boat surveys.
Visually identify and distinguish biological and physical features.

A completed online application showcasing how your qualifications align with the job requirements.
An up-to-date resume.

Description: In partnership with the Natural Resource Conservation Service (NRCS) and Pheasants Forever we are seeking a candidate who is motivated to build working relationships with farmers, associated agriculture advisors & consultants, and conservation partners.  Working in southeast Minnesota to prepare farm management plans that integrate conservation, agriculture, technology, and economics.  A goal of these farm management plans is to showcase alternative management practices that increase farm profitability and conservation opportunity.  Examples of alternative management practices that have been used successfully in Minnesota include cover crops, diverse crop rotation, hay plantings, variable rate inputs, prairie and shrub plantings, and wetland restoration.

In this agronomist type position, you will be responsible for one-on-one farm site visits, identifying and evaluating marginally productive cropland using agriculture technology, making maps and plans to improve areas on the farm, identifying & presenting grants and cost share opportunities, and monitoring project success.  Organizing and hosting workshops, field days, and other outreach efforts for public and professional audiences will further support farmer recruitment and is highly recommended.  Building and maintaining professional relationships within the agriculture community is paramount.

You will be a Pheasants Forever and Quail Forever employee based out of a United States Department of Agriculture (USDA) Service Center with regular travel within a ten-county coverage area. Overnight travel will be required.

*Once the candidate is trained and working independently, telework is allowable up to fifty percent of the time or as negotiated between candidate and manager.  During the training period, the candidate will need to report to their USDA office every day. *

Essential Job Duties:
Understand and relay how the use of economic information and precision data can be used to develop profitable conservation solutions on working lands.
Lead in the recruitment of farmers interested in conservation solutions.
Work cooperatively with Farm Bill Biologists to facilitate voluntary program identification, enrollment, and implementation.
Possess a working knowledge of data collection, management and software platforms to conduct and interpret analyses of precision data and economic inputs to calculate Return on Investment (ROI) and profitability at a sub-field level.

Description
Position Overview

The University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign (UIUC) invites applications for a Postdoctoral Research Associate to join an interdisciplinary research project investigating avian migration in the Intermountain West with large-scale bioacoustics approaches. This is a full-time appointment for one year with anticipated renewal for a second year, contingent on funding and job performance.

The postdoctoral researcher will play a leading role in analyzing an extensive acoustic dataset of migratory birds in western North America. The project integrates bioacoustic monitoring, machine learning-based species classification, landscape ecology, and weather and radar data to address fundamental and applied questions about bird migration. The position offers opportunities to lead multiple peer-reviewed publications and to collaborate with researchers at UIUC, MPG Ranch, and partner institutions. The postdoctoral researcher will be primarily supervised by Dr. Benjamin Van Doren, Assistant Professor in the Department of Natural Resources and Environmental Sciences (https://www.migrationbiology.org/).

Research Focus

This research will apply recent advances in AI-enabled bioacoustic analysis to a multi-year archive of passive acoustic recordings collected across a network of sites in the Intermountain West. The postdoctoral researcher will contribute to research aims that will include (1) landscape influences on migratory habitat use and (2) environmental drivers of migration decision-making. There may also be opportunities to pursue project extensions, such as incorporating additional acoustic datasets, modeling fine-scale migration flows, examining social dynamics of migrants, analyzing regional variation in vocalizations, or linking bioacoustic data with large-scale monitoring programs.

Responsibilities

Lead quantitative analyses of large-scale bioacoustic, environmental, and landscape datasets
Integrate acoustic data with radar, weather, and remote-sensing products
Develop and publish peer-reviewed manuscripts (expected 3–4 papers over the appointment)
Contribute to project coordination with research partners
Mentor graduate and undergraduate students 
Present findings at scientific conferences and workshops

Required Qualifications

Ph.D. in Ecology, Wildlife Biology, Conservation Biology, Computational Biology, or a related field 
Strong quantitative and analytical skills
Experience working with large ecological datasets
Proficiency in R and/or Python for data analysis
Demonstrated ability to lead scientific publications

Preferred Qualifications

Experience with bioacoustics, passive acoustic monitoring, or automated species classification
Familiarity with bird migration ecology
Experience integrating ecological data with weather, radar, or remote-sensing data
Background in spatial or landscape ecology
Interest in applied conservation questions

Salary and Benefits

The anticipated salary range is $55,000–$60,000, commensurate with experience. The position includes a comprehensive benefits package.

Remote Work Policy

Candidates able to work in person at UIUC will be preferred, but hybrid and remote work arrangements may be considered. 

University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign

UIUC is a leading public research university with a strong tradition of interdisciplinary scholarship. The campus hosts world-class programs in ecology, evolutionary biology, natural resources, computer science, and data science, providing a rich intellectual environment for collaborative research. Champaign-Urbana offers a high quality of life, a low cost of living, and a vibrant academic community.

Application Instructions

Applicants should submit the following documents to the form located at https://forms.gle/nRT7gXgsB5sASDuW8.

A cover letter describing research interests, relevant experience, and interest in this position
A curriculum vitae (CV)
Contact information for 3 references

Review of applications will begin immediately and continue until the position is filled. The anticipated start date is flexible. Please contact Dr. Benjamin Van Doren (vandoren@illinois.edu) with any questions about this position.
